summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it closes both routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.

The document problem predates the ban and is now absolute. Legal activists had been pressing for gender recognition reform for more than a decade on the grounds that official paperwork failing to match a person's identity made job applications difficult and exposed them to disclosure; from 2024 no recognition procedure is available at all, so a trans visitor's passport or ID will carry whatever marker their home jurisdiction issued, with no legal mechanism to alter it in Georgia and no lawful route to transition-related care if it is needed during the stay.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" measures, had raised fears of hate crimes in the country. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

Assembly rights were already constrained before the statutory ban. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in its planned city-centre locations on safety grounds, while organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march and far-right groups vowed to thwart it. Public LGBT assembly has since been prohibited outright.

The domestic protection machinery has been formally found wanting. A report submitted on 5 August 2024 by WISG and partner organisations to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions calls for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.
tangentialFactors:
The foreign agents law compounds the risk to support services. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that organisations refusing to register as "foreign agents" face fines or bankruptcy, a requirement that endangers LGBTI service provision across the country; the review also reports that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is circulating and that the anti-LGBTI law has eroded trust in institutions.

Georgia's package is described as the most severe of its kind in the South Caucasus, and it is being read alongside comparable "gay propaganda" legislation in a neighbouring jurisdiction rather than against regional practice. The consequences of that framing are diplomatic as well as domestic: the killing and the law were cited by European political figures as evidence that Georgia's EU accession path is being derailed.
localsOnly:
Residents face a service system under measurable strain. ILGA-Europe reports that applications to LGBTI services fell after the anti-LGBTI law, as trust eroded, and that large numbers of LGBTI people are leaving the country and seeking asylum documentation abroad.

Reporting and accountability gaps are documented rather than theoretical. The August 2024 report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers identifies hate-crime data collection as inadequate and calls for effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, alongside protection of assembly and expression. The recommendations were submitted as urgent and pending; the sources reviewed do not record their subsequent implementation.

Employment and identity documents remain a daily exposure for trans residents: where a person's gender identity does not match official paperwork, job applications become difficult, an obstacle that legal activists have been seeking to remedy through recognition reform since at least 2012 and which the 2024 law forecloses.
outOfScopeNotes:
Several points are unresolved on the sources reviewed. The specific offences and penalties attached to the 2024 law's bans on gender recognition, transition-related healthcare and LGBT assembly are not stated in the inventory, so the exact sanction a visitor would face is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening, the acceptance of foreign-issued identity markers at the border, or any risk of being flagged during arrival processing. Nor does the inventory record the outcome of the investigation into the killing of Kesaria Abramidze, including any hate-crime charges or conviction, or the current enforcement posture toward public assembly since the ban took effect.
